approachQuestion.prompt: Each reading has a non-negative value in values. Choose a set of positions with the greatest total value, with no two adjacent positions selected. Choosing nothing is allowed. Return only the greatest total, not the positions. Examples: [8,3,5,9,4] → 17; [6,10,6] → 12; [] → 0. Which approach handles the choices at neighboring positions?
constraints: Each values[i] is an integer from 0 to 1000000000.
The result fits in a signed 64-bit integer.

options.text: For decisions i=1…n, where the current value is values[i−1], compare best(i−1) with values[i−1]+best(i−2). Set best(0)=best(−1)=0, and keep only those two previous results.
options.feedback: Position i can be combined only with a prefix ending before i−1. For a numeric result, the two previous prefix optima are enough; the empty prefix and the prefix before it both have value zero.

options.text: Use the same “skip or take” comparison, but store the best result for every prefix in an array.
options.feedback: The recurrence is correct for every allowed input, but after computing a prefix, earlier results beyond the two latest are never read again. The output is only a sum, so storing the full history is unnecessary.

options.text: Repeatedly choose the largest available value, then remove that position and its neighbors.
options.feedback: A locally largest choice can block a better set. For [6,10,6], this method chooses 10, while positions 0 and 2 give 12.

options.text: Enumerate every subset of positions, discard subsets containing adjacent positions, and return the greatest sum.
options.feedback: This can return the right sum, but it checks each subset separately. Many different subsets share the same early choices, so those decisions are revisited from scratch.

feedback.reason: Consider what information must be kept between neighboring choices and whether the output requires recovering the selected positions.

complexityQuestion.prompt: Choose the time and auxiliary-space costs for the fixed method: for each decision i=1…n, compute max(best(i−1), values[i−1]+best(i−2)), with best(0)=best(−1)=0, then shift the two saved results. The method does not recover the selected positions. Let n = values.length.
constraints: Analyze the worst case. Each iteration and each operation on a 64-bit value takes constant time.
The input array and returned sum are not auxiliary space.
Auxiliary space includes every variable and data structure kept by the method.

feedback.reason: Each position is considered once, with a constant number of operations. The method keeps two prefix totals and a constant number of temporary values. The base cases return zero for empty input. Since the output is only the sum, no history is needed to recover positions.

messages.text: The fixed method does not enumerate subsets or branch recursively: it scans each of the n positions once, so this time bound is too large. Its live state also does not grow with n.
The time bound matches, but the fixed method keeps only two prefix totals and a constant number of temporary values. It does not store every prefix in a table.
The method makes one pass over the positions and does constant work at each position, so this time bound is too large even though the space component matches.

methodReveal.title: The skip-or-take state for a prefix
methodReveal.description: For decision i=1…n, compare the best total without the current position with its value values[i−1] plus the best total before the previous position. Set best(0)=best(−1)=0, then keep the new optimum and the previous optimum. The output contains only the total, so the selected positions are not recovered.
